one_liner: D matmul in kostya/benchmarks: Phobos dotProduct's two partial sums run about 2x faster than the suite's single-accumulator C loop.
what_it_does: matmul/matmul.d allocates two 1500x1500 double matrices as GC-allocated jagged arrays, transposes the second, and fills each output cell with std.numeric.dotProduct(arow, crow); the C version (matmul/matmul.c) does the same transpose but computes each cell with a plain one-accumulator loop. The reusable piece is Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct, a standard-library function over two slices, not a D language feature or a matmul library.
how_it_is_fast: dotProduct (std/numeric.d) walks the arrays through raw pointers in 16-element blocks, alternating products into two accumulators (sum0, sum1), then 4-element blocks, then a scalar tail, so the loop carries two independent floating-point add chains instead of one. The C, Rust, Zig and Nim loops keep a single accumulator under strict IEEE semantics (no -ffast-math), so the compiler can neither reassociate nor vectorize the reduction and every iteration waits on the previous add. Halving the dependency chain roughly halves the time: C at 3.034 s versus gdc at 1.505 s (derivation from the table, not stated by the suite).
when_to_use: As a demonstration that multiple partial sums matter for strict-FP reductions: any dot-product or sum loop compiled without -ffast-math is latency-bound on one accumulator
D code that needs a portable, dependency-free dot product of double or float slices: std.numeric.dotProduct is already in Phobos and beats a hand-written single-accumulator loop
Small or medium vectors where linking BLAS is not worth it and a few-ulp change in summation order is acceptable
when_not_to_use: As evidence that D beats C: in attractivechaos/plb2, with the same i-k-j loop in both languages on Apple M1, D ldc2 1.35.0 takes 0.57 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s
Real matrix multiplication: in the same table the BLAS-backed D/ldc2 (lubeck) row runs in 0.042 s and C++ Eigen in 0.081 s, about 36x and 19x faster than D/gdc
When bit-for-bit agreement with a sequential reference sum is required: two partial sums change rounding
When the C side can be changed: two or more accumulators, or -ffast-math or -fassociative-math, in C give the same effect without switching language

integration.dependencies: none beyond Phobos and druntime (std.numeric); the benchmark program also uses the GC for its matrices
integration.min_toolchain: any current D compiler; measured with gdc 14.2.0, ldc2 1.41.0 and dmd v2.111.0
integration.platforms: any (portable scalar D, no intrinsics); measured on x86-64 Intel Xeon E-2324G
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the function reads two const slices and keeps only local state

gotchas: Not like for like: the C, Rust, Zig and Nim versions that tie at about 3.03-3.12 s each use one accumulator, while the D program calls a hand-unrolled two-accumulator library kernel; the results therefore differ in the last bits, and the harness self-test only checks calc(101) within 0.1 of -18.67.
Flags favour C, not D: C gets -O3 -march=native -flto=auto from common/commands.mk, the D builds have no -march and no LTO, so the D lead is not a codegen advantage.

The D/gdc row reports a peak RSS increase of 4.00 MiB while D/ldc2 and D/dmd report 70.38 MiB for the same four 1500x1500 matrices (xtime.rb samples /proc/PID/statm every 10 ms); the suite gives no explanation, so treat the gdc memory column as unreliable.
The timed region (between the notify start and stop messages) includes matrix generation, GC allocation and the transpose, not only the multiply.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Unlike the Fortran plb2 sibling (same i-k-j loop as C, 0.51 s versus 0.54 s) this is not a language-level win, so pick it only as the two-accumulator lesson or when you are already writing D; for actual matrix products, BLAS wrappers and Julia packages in the category (Gaius.jl and the lubeck row) are far faster.
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks (README updated 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G, medians) times 1500x1500 double matmul at 1.505 s for D/gdc 14.2.0, 1.722 s for D/ldc2 1.41.0 and 1.880 s for D/dmd 2.111.0 versus 3.034 s for C/gcc 16.1.0 and 3.067 s for C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto), so about 2.0x, 1.76x and 1.61x (derived from page data); the gap comes from Phobos dotProduct's two partial sums against a one-accumulator strict-FP C loop.
status_note: kostya/benchmarks is active (2.9k stars, MIT, results refreshed 2026-07-19) and std.numeric.dotProduct ships with every D compiler, but the entry documents a kernel difference rather than a reusable D advantage.
